So he dismounted, tied his mount, drew his sword, and entered through the gate of the fortress. [(p-114)] When he entered the fortress, he found two enormous gates [he had never seen larger], and the two gates were inlaid with red [and white] rubies. When he saw this he was astonished, and he opened one of the two gates, and there was a city the like of which no one had ever seen. There were palaces, and each palace had upper chambers, and above the upper chambers were more chambers, built of gold, silver, pearls and rubies. The doors of those chambers were like the doors of the city, facing one another, and all of them were carpeted with pearls, with knobs of musk and saffron. When he beheld this, and saw no one, he was overwhelmed. Then he looked at the alleys, and in every alley there were trees laden with fruit, and beneath the trees were flowing rivers whose water ran through channels of silver. The man said: "This must be Paradise." He took with him some of its pearls and some of the musk and saffron knobs, and returned to Yemen, and he displayed what he had with him. The matter reached Mu'awiyah, who sent for him, and he related to him what he had seen. Mu'awiyah then sent for Ka'b al-Ahbar, and when he came, Mu'awiyah said to him: "O Abu Ishaq, is there in this world a city of gold and silver?" He replied: "Yes, I will tell you about it and about the one who built it. It was built by Shaddad ibn Ad, and the city is: [(p-115)] ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾." He said: "Then tell me its story." He said: "Ad, to whom the first 'Ad' is ascribed, had two sons: Shadid and Shaddad. When Ad died, and then Shadid died and Shaddad remained, he ruled the earth, and kings submitted to him. He was fond of reading books, and whenever he came across a description of Paradise, his soul urged him to build its like, out of defiance toward God, exalted is He. So he ordered the making of ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, and he appointed over its construction a hundred qahramans (chief stewards), each with a thousand assistants. He wrote to the kings of the earth that they should supply him with the jewels found in their lands. The qahramans set out traveling through the earth to find a suitable land, and they came upon a vast, pure desert, free of hills, in which there were springs of water and meadows. They said: 'This is the description of the land in which the king commanded that it be built.' So they laid its foundation of Yemeni onyx, and they spent three hundred years in its construction, while Shaddad's lifespan was nine hundred years. When they came to him, having finished it, he said: 'Go, and make a fortress for it, and place around the fortress a thousand palaces, [(p-116)] with a thousand banners beside each palace, so that in each of those palaces there will be a vizier from my viziers.' They did so. Then the king commanded the viziers, who numbered a thousand, to prepare for the move to ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾. The king and his household spent ten years in preparation, then they set out for it. When they were a day and a night's journey from it, God sent upon him and upon all who were with him a cry from the sky, and it destroyed them all, and not one of them remained."

[(p-116)] Al-Sha'bi narrated from Daghfal al-Shaybani, from the scholars of Himyar, who said: "When Shaddad ibn Ad and those with him perished by the cry, his son Martad ibn Shaddad became king after him. His father had left him in Hadramawt in charge of his rule and authority. He ordered that his father be carried from that wasteland to Hadramawt, and ordered that he be buried. A pit was dug for him in the wasteland, and he deposited him there upon a golden throne, and cast over him seventy robes woven with golden threads. He placed at his head a great golden tablet, on which he inscribed:

Take heed, O deceived one, with your long life,
I am Shaddad ibn Ad, lord of the lofty fortress,
And brother of strength, and of might, and of vast dominion.
[(p-117)] The people of the earth, all of them, submitted to me out of fear of my threat.
I possessed the East and the West with a mighty authority,
And with the bounty of dominion and its numbers and multitudes.
Then came Hud, while we were in error before Hud.
He called us, if we had accepted him, to the right course.
We disobeyed him, and he called out: 'What is wrong with you? Is there any escape?'
Then a cry came upon us, screaming from the distant horizon,
So we were gathered like a crop in a barren, reaped plain.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Thamud, who hewed the rock﴾: they cut it and dug into it. Ishaq said: "The valley" is the Valley of the Villages. Al-Hasan recited "bil-wadi" with the yā' retained in both states. ﴿And Pharaoh of the stakes﴾ is explained in Surah Sad [38:12]. ﴿Who transgressed in the lands﴾ means: Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, who committed sins and acted tyrannically toward the prophets of God. ﴿And multiplied corruption therein﴾: killing and sins. ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. [(p-118)] Ibn Qutaybah said: He said "a scourge of punishment" because punishment may be by means of a whip. Al-Zajjaj said: [meaning, He made the whip with which He struck them the punishment]. ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾: He watches over whoever disbelieves in Him, to punish him. The "marsad" is the path, and we have explained it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is an ambush﴾ [an-Naba' 78:21].

[p. 102]

**Surah al-Fajr (The Dawn)**

It is Meccan in its entirety, by scholarly consensus.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the dawn﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-Fajr is the breaking forth of darkness into morning. And "infajara al-ma'" means the water gushed forth. Our shaykh ʿAli ibn ʿUbayd Allah said: al-Fajr is the light of day when the night is split open by it. It derives from al-infijar (bursting forth). One says: "infajara al-nahr yanfajiru infijaran" when a place in it is split open for the water to come out. From this, the wrongdoer (al-fajir) is so called, because he has departed from the obedience of God.

The exegetes have six opinions regarding the intended meaning of this dawn.

[p. 103] The first: it is the well-known dawn, which is the beginning of the day. This was said by ʿAli, may God be pleased with him. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: it is the breaking forth of the morning every day. ʿIkrimah, Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Qurazi also said this.

The second: it is the dawn prayer (ṣalat al-fajr). Ataʾ narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it is the entire day, and it is referred to by "dawn" because it is its beginning. Abu Nasr narrated this meaning from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: it is specifically the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). Mujahid said this.

The fifth: it is the dawn of the first day of Dhu al-Hijjah. al-Dahhak said this.

The sixth: it is the first day of Muharram, from which the year bursts forth. Qatadah said this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ten nights﴾. Regarding it there are four opinions.

The first: they are the ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah. al-ʿAwfi narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Muqatil said it too.

[p. 104] The second: they are the last ten nights of Ramadan. Abu Zabyan narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: they are the first ten nights of Ramadan. al-Dahhak said this.

The fourth: they are the first ten nights of Muharram. Yaman ibn Riʾab said this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisaʾi and Khalaf read "wal-witr" with a kasra on the waw, while the rest read it with a fatha. Both are dialectal forms (lughatan). al-Farraʾ said: the kasra belongs to Quraysh, Tamim and Asad, and the fatha to the people of the Hijaz.

Regarding "al-shafʿ wal-witr" (the even and the odd), the exegetes have twenty opinions.

The first: al-shafʿ is the Day of ʿArafah and the Day of Sacrifice, and al-witr is the night of sacrifice (laylat al-nahr). Abu Ayyub al-Ansari narrated it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The second: al-shafʿ is the Day of Sacrifice, and al-witr is the Day of ʿArafah. [Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak also said it.]

[p. 105] The third: al-shafʿ and al-witr are the prayer, of which some is even (shafʿ) and some is odd (witr). ʿImran ibn Husayn narrated it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and Qatadah said it.

[p. 106] The fourth: [al-shafʿ is all creation, and al-witr is God, exalted is He]. al-ʿAwfi narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. Mujahid said it according to the narration of Masruq, and Abu Salih said it.

The fifth: al-witr is Adam, who was made even (shufiʿa) with his wife. Mujahid narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The sixth: al-shafʿ is the two days after the Day of Sacrifice, which is the first departure (al-nafr al-awwal), and al-witr is the third day, which is the final departure (al-nafr al-akhir). ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said this, citing His saying: ﴿But whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203].

The seventh: al-shafʿ is the morning prayer, and al-witr is the sunset prayer. ʿAtiyyah related it.

The eighth: al-shafʿ is the two rakʿahs of the sunset prayer, and al-witr is the third rakʿah. Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said this.

The ninth: al-shafʿ and al-witr are all creation: some of it is even and some of it is odd. Ibn Zayd said this, and Mujahid in one narration.

The tenth: it is number, some of which is even and some odd. This and the preceding opinion are narrated from al-Hasan.

The eleventh: al-shafʿ is the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-witr is the three days of [Mina]. al-Dahhak said this.

[p. 107] The twelfth: al-shafʿ is God, based on His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7], and al-witr is God, based on His saying: ﴿Say, He is God, the One﴾. Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah said this.

The thirteenth: al-shafʿ is Adam and Eve, and al-witr is God, exalted is He. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said this.

The fourteenth: al-shafʿ is the days and nights, and al-witr is the day after which there is no night, which is the Day of Resurrection. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said this.

The fifteenth: al-shafʿ is the levels of Paradise, since there are eight, and al-witr is the levels of Hell, since there are seven. So it is as if God swore by Paradise and Hell. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said this.

The sixteenth: al-shafʿ is the contrariety of the attributes of created beings: between honour and humiliation, power and weakness, strength and frailty, knowledge and ignorance, death and life. And al-witr is the singularity of God's attributes: honour without humiliation, power without weakness, strength without frailty, knowledge without ignorance, and life without death. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said this.

The seventeenth: al-shafʿ is al-Safa and al-Marwah, and al-witr is the House (al-Bayt).

The eighteenth: al-shafʿ is the Mosque of Mecca and the Mosque of Medina, and al-witr is the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

The nineteenth: al-shafʿ is combining the Hajj with the tamattuʿ (combined pilgrimage, performing ʿumrah then Hajj), and al-witr is the ifrad (performing Hajj alone).

The twentieth: al-shafʿ is the acts of worship that recur, such as prayer, fasting and zakat, [p. 108] and al-witr is the act of worship that does not recur, which is the Hajj. al-Thaʿlabi related these four opinions.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾. Ibn Kathir and Yaʿqub read "yasri" with a yaʾ in both pause and continuation. Nafiʿ and Abu ʿAmr agreed with them in continuation. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim, Hamzah and al-Kisaʾi read "yasr" without a yaʾ in both continuation and pause. al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj said: the preferred reading is to omit it, to match the ends of the verses and to follow the codex (al-mushaf, the standard written Qur'an). Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: the action belongs to the night, and within this there are two views. One: "idha yasri" means going away, which is said by the majority, and is the preference of al-Zajjaj. The second: "idha yasri" means approaching, which is said by Qatadah.

The second opinion: the action belongs to something else, and the meaning is "when it is traversed in," as one says "a sleeping night" (layl naʾim), meaning one sleeps in it. al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutaybah said this.

Regarding the intended meaning of this night there are three opinions.

The first: it is general to every night, and this is the apparent meaning.

The second: it is the night of Muzdalifah, which is the night of Jamʿ (gathering), said by Mujahid and ʿIkrimah.

The third: it is the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr), related by al-Mawardi.

[p. 109] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ That is: [is there in that which has been mentioned of these matters by which We have sworn] ﴿an oath for one of understanding﴾, that is, for one of intellect. Intellect is called ḥijr (restraint), because it restrains its possessor from what is ugly. It is called ʿaql (reason), because it restrains (yaʿqilu) from what is not becoming. And intellect is called al-nuhā (the faculty of restraint), because it forbids what is not lawful. The meaning of the statement is: whoever has understanding knows that what God has sworn by among these things contains proofs of God's oneness and power, so it is fitting that He swear by it because of what it indicates. The response of the oath is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾. Between the oath and its response is inserted His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿAd﴾, thereby warning the people of Mecca with the destruction of those who were stronger than them. Ibn Masʿud and Ibn Yaʿmar read "bi-ʿAdi Iram" with a kasra on the dal, without tanwin, as an idafah (construct).

Regarding "Iram" there are four opinions.

The first: it is the name of a town, said al-Farraʾ. "Iram" is not declined because it is the name of a town. Regarding this town there are three opinions. One: it is Damascus, said by Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, ʿIkrimah, [p. 110] and Khalid al-Rabʿi. Two: it is Alexandria, said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb. Three: it is a city built by Shaddad ibn ʿAd, and this is the saying of Kaʿb. Its mention will come, God willing.

The second opinion: it is the name of a nation among the nations, and its meaning is "the ancient," said by Mujahid.

The third: it is a tribe from the people of ʿAd, said by Qatadah and Muqatil. al-Zajjaj said: [p. 111] "Iram" is not declined because it was made the name of a tribe and thus given the fatha, and it is in the position of a genitive.

The fourth: it is the name of the grandfather of ʿAd, since he was ʿAd ibn ʿAws ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Ibn Ishaq said this. al-Farraʾ said: if it is the name of a man according to this view, then it is left undeclined because it is like a non-Arabic name. Abu ʿUbaydah said: there were two ʿAds. The first is Iram, and it is the one of whom God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿAd﴾ [al-Najm: 50].

Whether the people of Hud were the first ʿAd or not, there are two opinions, which we have mentioned in the commentary on al-Najm.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ there are four opinions.

The first: they were people of pillars and tents, seeking pasture wherever it was, then returning to their dwellings, so they did not settle in one place. ʿAtaʾ narrated this meaning from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Farraʾ said it too.

The second: the meaning of "dhat al-ʿimad" is "the tall one." This was also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Muqatil and Abu ʿUbaydah said it. al-Zajjaj said: one says "rajulun muʿammad" when a man is tall.

[p. 112] The third: "possessor of strength and might," derived from the strength of pillars, said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: "possessor of a firmly built structure with pillars," said by Ibn Zayd. It was also said that they were called "possessors of pillars" because of a building that one of them constructed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The like of which was not created in the lands﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawzaʾ and Abu ʿImran read "lam tukhlaq" with a fatha on the ta and a raf (nominative) on the lam of "mithluha" in the accusative... [transcription: they read "lam takhluq" with an open ta and a nominative lam, "mithlaha" with an accusative lam].

Muʿadh al-Qari and ʿAmr ibn Dinar read "lam nakhluq" with an open nun and a nominative lam, "mithlaha" with an accusative lam.

Regarding what is referred to (al-mushar ilayha) there are two opinions.

One: the like of that tribe was not created in tallness and strength. This is the meaning of al-Hasan's saying.

The second: the city. The like of their city, possessing pillars, was not created. ʿIkrimah said this.

Descriptions of that city have come in the tafsir, and this indication refers to that.

[(p-113)] Wahb ibn Munabbih narrated from Abdullah ibn Qilabah that he set out in search of a camel of his that had strayed. While he was in the deserts of Aden, he came upon a city in those wastelands with a fortress, and around the fortress were many palaces. When he drew near it, he thought there might be someone in it who could tell him about his camel, but he saw no one coming out or going in. So he dismounted, tied his mount, drew his sword, and entered through the gate of the fortress. [(p-114)] When he entered the fortress, he found two enormous gates [he had never seen larger], and the two gates were inlaid with red [and white] rubies. When he saw this he was astonished, and he opened one of the two gates, and there was a city the like of which no one had ever seen. There were palaces, and each palace had upper chambers, and above the upper chambers were more chambers, built of gold, silver, pearls and rubies. The doors of those chambers were like the doors of the city, facing one another, and all of them were carpeted with pearls, with knobs of musk and saffron. When he beheld this, and saw no one, he was overwhelmed. Then he looked at the alleys, and in every alley there were trees laden with fruit, and beneath the trees were flowing rivers whose water ran through channels of silver. The man said: "This must be Paradise." He took with him some of its pearls and some of the musk and saffron knobs, and returned to Yemen, and he displayed what he had with him. The matter reached Mu'awiyah, who sent for him, and he related to him what he had seen. Mu'awiyah then sent for Ka'b al-Ahbar, and when he came, Mu'awiyah said to him: "O Abu Ishaq, is there in this world a city of gold and silver?" He replied: "Yes, I will tell you about it and about the one who built it. It was built by Shaddad ibn Ad, and the city is: [(p-115)] ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾." He said: "Then tell me its story." He said: "Ad, to whom the first 'Ad' is ascribed, had two sons: Shadid and Shaddad. When Ad died, and then Shadid died and Shaddad remained, he ruled the earth, and kings submitted to him. He was fond of reading books, and whenever he came across a description of Paradise, his soul urged him to build its like, out of defiance toward God, exalted is He. So he ordered the making of ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, and he appointed over its construction a hundred qahramans (chief stewards), each with a thousand assistants. He wrote to the kings of the earth that they should supply him with the jewels found in their lands. The qahramans set out traveling through the earth to find a suitable land, and they came upon a vast, pure desert, free of hills, in which there were springs of water and meadows. They said: 'This is the description of the land in which the king commanded that it be built.' So they laid its foundation of Yemeni onyx, and they spent three hundred years in its construction, while Shaddad's lifespan was nine hundred years. When they came to him, having finished it, he said: 'Go, and make a fortress for it, and place around the fortress a thousand palaces, [(p-116)] with a thousand banners beside each palace, so that in each of those palaces there will be a vizier from my viziers.' They did so. Then the king commanded the viziers, who numbered a thousand, to prepare for the move to ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾. The king and his household spent ten years in preparation, then they set out for it. When they were a day and a night's journey from it, God sent upon him and upon all who were with him a cry from the sky, and it destroyed them all, and not one of them remained."

[(p-116)] Al-Sha'bi narrated from Daghfal al-Shaybani, from the scholars of Himyar, who said: "When Shaddad ibn Ad and those with him perished by the cry, his son Martad ibn Shaddad became king after him. His father had left him in Hadramawt in charge of his rule and authority. He ordered that his father be carried from that wasteland to Hadramawt, and ordered that he be buried. A pit was dug for him in the wasteland, and he deposited him there upon a golden throne, and cast over him seventy robes woven with golden threads. He placed at his head a great golden tablet, on which he inscribed:

Take heed, O deceived one, with your long life,
I am Shaddad ibn Ad, lord of the lofty fortress,
And brother of strength, and of might, and of vast dominion.
[(p-117)] The people of the earth, all of them, submitted to me out of fear of my threat.
I possessed the East and the West with a mighty authority,
And with the bounty of dominion and its numbers and multitudes.
Then came Hud, while we were in error before Hud.
He called us, if we had accepted him, to the right course.
We disobeyed him, and he called out: 'What is wrong with you? Is there any escape?'
Then a cry came upon us, screaming from the distant horizon,
So we were gathered like a crop in a barren, reaped plain.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Thamud, who hewed the rock﴾: they cut it and dug into it. Ishaq said: "The valley" is the Valley of the Villages. Al-Hasan recited "bil-wadi" with the yā' retained in both states. ﴿And Pharaoh of the stakes﴾ is explained in Surah Sad [38:12]. ﴿Who transgressed in the lands﴾ means: Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, who committed sins and acted tyrannically toward the prophets of God. ﴿And multiplied corruption therein﴾: killing and sins. ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. [(p-118)] Ibn Qutaybah said: He said "a scourge of punishment" because punishment may be by means of a whip. Al-Zajjaj said: [meaning, He made the whip with which He struck them the punishment]. ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾: He watches over whoever disbelieves in Him, to punish him. The "marsad" is the path, and we have explained it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is an ambush﴾ [an-Naba' 78:21].

[p. 102]

**Surah al-Fajr (The Dawn)**

It is Meccan in its entirety, by scholarly consensus.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the dawn﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-Fajr is the breaking forth of darkness into morning. And "infajara al-ma'" means the water gushed forth. Our shaykh ʿAli ibn ʿUbayd Allah said: al-Fajr is the light of day when the night is split open by it. It derives from al-infijar (bursting forth). One says: "infajara al-nahr yanfajiru infijaran" when a place in it is split open for the water to come out. From this, the wrongdoer (al-fajir) is so called, because he has departed from the obedience of God.

The exegetes have six opinions regarding the intended meaning of this dawn.

[p. 103] The first: it is the well-known dawn, which is the beginning of the day. This was said by ʿAli, may God be pleased with him. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: it is the breaking forth of the morning every day. ʿIkrimah, Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Qurazi also said this.

The second: it is the dawn prayer (ṣalat al-fajr). Ataʾ narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it is the entire day, and it is referred to by "dawn" because it is its beginning. Abu Nasr narrated this meaning from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: it is specifically the dawn of the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). Mujahid said this.

The fifth: it is the dawn of the first day of Dhu al-Hijjah. al-Dahhak said this.

The sixth: it is the first day of Muharram, from which the year bursts forth. Qatadah said this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And ten nights﴾. Regarding it there are four opinions.

The first: they are the ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah. al-ʿAwfi narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and Muqatil said it too.

[p. 104] The second: they are the last ten nights of Ramadan. Abu Zabyan narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: they are the first ten nights of Ramadan. al-Dahhak said this.

The fourth: they are the first ten nights of Muharram. Yaman ibn Riʾab said this.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the even and the odd﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisaʾi and Khalaf read "wal-witr" with a kasra on the waw, while the rest read it with a fatha. Both are dialectal forms (lughatan). al-Farraʾ said: the kasra belongs to Quraysh, Tamim and Asad, and the fatha to the people of the Hijaz.

Regarding "al-shafʿ wal-witr" (the even and the odd), the exegetes have twenty opinions.

The first: al-shafʿ is the Day of ʿArafah and the Day of Sacrifice, and al-witr is the night of sacrifice (laylat al-nahr). Abu Ayyub al-Ansari narrated it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The second: al-shafʿ is the Day of Sacrifice, and al-witr is the Day of ʿArafah. [Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak also said it.]

[p. 105] The third: al-shafʿ and al-witr are the prayer, of which some is even (shafʿ) and some is odd (witr). ʿImran ibn Husayn narrated it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and Qatadah said it.

[p. 106] The fourth: [al-shafʿ is all creation, and al-witr is God, exalted is He]. al-ʿAwfi narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas. Mujahid said it according to the narration of Masruq, and Abu Salih said it.

The fifth: al-witr is Adam, who was made even (shufiʿa) with his wife. Mujahid narrated it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The sixth: al-shafʿ is the two days after the Day of Sacrifice, which is the first departure (al-nafr al-awwal), and al-witr is the third day, which is the final departure (al-nafr al-akhir). ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr said this, citing His saying: ﴿But whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 203].

The seventh: al-shafʿ is the morning prayer, and al-witr is the sunset prayer. ʿAtiyyah related it.

The eighth: al-shafʿ is the two rakʿahs of the sunset prayer, and al-witr is the third rakʿah. Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said this.

The ninth: al-shafʿ and al-witr are all creation: some of it is even and some of it is odd. Ibn Zayd said this, and Mujahid in one narration.

The tenth: it is number, some of which is even and some odd. This and the preceding opinion are narrated from al-Hasan.

The eleventh: al-shafʿ is the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-witr is the three days of [Mina]. al-Dahhak said this.

[p. 107] The twelfth: al-shafʿ is God, based on His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7], and al-witr is God, based on His saying: ﴿Say, He is God, the One﴾. Sufyan ibn ʿUyaynah said this.

The thirteenth: al-shafʿ is Adam and Eve, and al-witr is God, exalted is He. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said this.

The fourteenth: al-shafʿ is the days and nights, and al-witr is the day after which there is no night, which is the Day of Resurrection. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said this.

The fifteenth: al-shafʿ is the levels of Paradise, since there are eight, and al-witr is the levels of Hell, since there are seven. So it is as if God swore by Paradise and Hell. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said this.

The sixteenth: al-shafʿ is the contrariety of the attributes of created beings: between honour and humiliation, power and weakness, strength and frailty, knowledge and ignorance, death and life. And al-witr is the singularity of God's attributes: honour without humiliation, power without weakness, strength without frailty, knowledge without ignorance, and life without death. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said this.

The seventeenth: al-shafʿ is al-Safa and al-Marwah, and al-witr is the House (al-Bayt).

The eighteenth: al-shafʿ is the Mosque of Mecca and the Mosque of Medina, and al-witr is the Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

The nineteenth: al-shafʿ is combining the Hajj with the tamattuʿ (combined pilgrimage, performing ʿumrah then Hajj), and al-witr is the ifrad (performing Hajj alone).

The twentieth: al-shafʿ is the acts of worship that recur, such as prayer, fasting and zakat, [p. 108] and al-witr is the act of worship that does not recur, which is the Hajj. al-Thaʿlabi related these four opinions.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾. Ibn Kathir and Yaʿqub read "yasri" with a yaʾ in both pause and continuation. Nafiʿ and Abu ʿAmr agreed with them in continuation. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim, Hamzah and al-Kisaʾi read "yasr" without a yaʾ in both continuation and pause. al-Farraʾ and al-Zajjaj said: the preferred reading is to omit it, to match the ends of the verses and to follow the codex (al-mushaf, the standard written Qur'an). Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the night when it passes﴾, there are two opinions.

The first: the action belongs to the night, and within this there are two views. One: "idha yasri" means going away, which is said by the majority, and is the preference of al-Zajjaj. The second: "idha yasri" means approaching, which is said by Qatadah.

The second opinion: the action belongs to something else, and the meaning is "when it is traversed in," as one says "a sleeping night" (layl naʾim), meaning one sleeps in it. al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutaybah said this.

Regarding the intended meaning of this night there are three opinions.

The first: it is general to every night, and this is the apparent meaning.

The second: it is the night of Muzdalifah, which is the night of Jamʿ (gathering), said by Mujahid and ʿIkrimah.

The third: it is the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr), related by al-Mawardi.

[p. 109] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is there in that an oath for one of understanding?﴾ That is: [is there in that which has been mentioned of these matters by which We have sworn] ﴿an oath for one of understanding﴾, that is, for one of intellect. Intellect is called ḥijr (restraint), because it restrains its possessor from what is ugly. It is called ʿaql (reason), because it restrains (yaʿqilu) from what is not becoming. And intellect is called al-nuhā (the faculty of restraint), because it forbids what is not lawful. The meaning of the statement is: whoever has understanding knows that what God has sworn by among these things contains proofs of God's oneness and power, so it is fitting that He swear by it because of what it indicates. The response of the oath is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾. Between the oath and its response is inserted His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿAd﴾, thereby warning the people of Mecca with the destruction of those who were stronger than them. Ibn Masʿud and Ibn Yaʿmar read "bi-ʿAdi Iram" with a kasra on the dal, without tanwin, as an idafah (construct).

Regarding "Iram" there are four opinions.

The first: it is the name of a town, said al-Farraʾ. "Iram" is not declined because it is the name of a town. Regarding this town there are three opinions. One: it is Damascus, said by Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, ʿIkrimah, [p. 110] and Khalid al-Rabʿi. Two: it is Alexandria, said by Muhammad ibn Kaʿb. Three: it is a city built by Shaddad ibn ʿAd, and this is the saying of Kaʿb. Its mention will come, God willing.

The second opinion: it is the name of a nation among the nations, and its meaning is "the ancient," said by Mujahid.

The third: it is a tribe from the people of ʿAd, said by Qatadah and Muqatil. al-Zajjaj said: [p. 111] "Iram" is not declined because it was made the name of a tribe and thus given the fatha, and it is in the position of a genitive.

The fourth: it is the name of the grandfather of ʿAd, since he was ʿAd ibn ʿAws ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Ibn Ishaq said this. al-Farraʾ said: if it is the name of a man according to this view, then it is left undeclined because it is like a non-Arabic name. Abu ʿUbaydah said: there were two ʿAds. The first is Iram, and it is the one of whom God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And that He destroyed the first ʿAd﴾ [al-Najm: 50].

Whether the people of Hud were the first ʿAd or not, there are two opinions, which we have mentioned in the commentary on al-Najm.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ there are four opinions.

The first: they were people of pillars and tents, seeking pasture wherever it was, then returning to their dwellings, so they did not settle in one place. ʿAtaʾ narrated this meaning from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Farraʾ said it too.

The second: the meaning of "dhat al-ʿimad" is "the tall one." This was also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Muqatil and Abu ʿUbaydah said it. al-Zajjaj said: one says "rajulun muʿammad" when a man is tall.

[p. 112] The third: "possessor of strength and might," derived from the strength of pillars, said by al-Dahhak.

The fourth: "possessor of a firmly built structure with pillars," said by Ibn Zayd. It was also said that they were called "possessors of pillars" because of a building that one of them constructed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The like of which was not created in the lands﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawzaʾ and Abu ʿImran read "lam tukhlaq" with a fatha on the ta and a raf (nominative) on the lam of "mithluha" in the accusative... [transcription: they read "lam takhluq" with an open ta and a nominative lam, "mithlaha" with an accusative lam].

Muʿadh al-Qari and ʿAmr ibn Dinar read "lam nakhluq" with an open nun and a nominative lam, "mithlaha" with an accusative lam.

Regarding what is referred to (al-mushar ilayha) there are two opinions.

One: the like of that tribe was not created in tallness and strength. This is the meaning of al-Hasan's saying.

The second: the city. The like of their city, possessing pillars, was not created. ʿIkrimah said this.

Descriptions of that city have come in the tafsir, and this indication refers to that.

[(p-113)] Wahb ibn Munabbih narrated from Abdullah ibn Qilabah that he set out in search of a camel of his that had strayed. While he was in the deserts of Aden, he came upon a city in those wastelands with a fortress, and around the fortress were many palaces. When he drew near it, he thought there might be someone in it who could tell him about his camel, but he saw no one coming out or going in. So he dismounted, tied his mount, drew his sword, and entered through the gate of the fortress. [(p-114)] When he entered the fortress, he found two enormous gates [he had never seen larger], and the two gates were inlaid with red [and white] rubies. When he saw this he was astonished, and he opened one of the two gates, and there was a city the like of which no one had ever seen. There were palaces, and each palace had upper chambers, and above the upper chambers were more chambers, built of gold, silver, pearls and rubies. The doors of those chambers were like the doors of the city, facing one another, and all of them were carpeted with pearls, with knobs of musk and saffron. When he beheld this, and saw no one, he was overwhelmed. Then he looked at the alleys, and in every alley there were trees laden with fruit, and beneath the trees were flowing rivers whose water ran through channels of silver. The man said: "This must be Paradise." He took with him some of its pearls and some of the musk and saffron knobs, and returned to Yemen, and he displayed what he had with him. The matter reached Mu'awiyah, who sent for him, and he related to him what he had seen. Mu'awiyah then sent for Ka'b al-Ahbar, and when he came, Mu'awiyah said to him: "O Abu Ishaq, is there in this world a city of gold and silver?" He replied: "Yes, I will tell you about it and about the one who built it. It was built by Shaddad ibn Ad, and the city is: [(p-115)] ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾." He said: "Then tell me its story." He said: "Ad, to whom the first 'Ad' is ascribed, had two sons: Shadid and Shaddad. When Ad died, and then Shadid died and Shaddad remained, he ruled the earth, and kings submitted to him. He was fond of reading books, and whenever he came across a description of Paradise, his soul urged him to build its like, out of defiance toward God, exalted is He. So he ordered the making of ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, and he appointed over its construction a hundred qahramans (chief stewards), each with a thousand assistants. He wrote to the kings of the earth that they should supply him with the jewels found in their lands. The qahramans set out traveling through the earth to find a suitable land, and they came upon a vast, pure desert, free of hills, in which there were springs of water and meadows. They said: 'This is the description of the land in which the king commanded that it be built.' So they laid its foundation of Yemeni onyx, and they spent three hundred years in its construction, while Shaddad's lifespan was nine hundred years. When they came to him, having finished it, he said: 'Go, and make a fortress for it, and place around the fortress a thousand palaces, [(p-116)] with a thousand banners beside each palace, so that in each of those palaces there will be a vizier from my viziers.' They did so. Then the king commanded the viziers, who numbered a thousand, to prepare for the move to ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾. The king and his household spent ten years in preparation, then they set out for it. When they were a day and a night's journey from it, God sent upon him and upon all who were with him a cry from the sky, and it destroyed them all, and not one of them remained."

[(p-116)] Al-Sha'bi narrated from Daghfal al-Shaybani, from the scholars of Himyar, who said: "When Shaddad ibn Ad and those with him perished by the cry, his son Martad ibn Shaddad became king after him. His father had left him in Hadramawt in charge of his rule and authority. He ordered that his father be carried from that wasteland to Hadramawt, and ordered that he be buried. A pit was dug for him in the wasteland, and he deposited him there upon a golden throne, and cast over him seventy robes woven with golden threads. He placed at his head a great golden tablet, on which he inscribed:

Take heed, O deceived one, with your long life,
I am Shaddad ibn Ad, lord of the lofty fortress,
And brother of strength, and of might, and of vast dominion.
[(p-117)] The people of the earth, all of them, submitted to me out of fear of my threat.
I possessed the East and the West with a mighty authority,
And with the bounty of dominion and its numbers and multitudes.
Then came Hud, while we were in error before Hud.
He called us, if we had accepted him, to the right course.
We disobeyed him, and he called out: 'What is wrong with you? Is there any escape?'
Then a cry came upon us, screaming from the distant horizon,
So we were gathered like a crop in a barren, reaped plain.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Thamud, who hewed the rock﴾: they cut it and dug into it. Ishaq said: "The valley" is the Valley of the Villages. Al-Hasan recited "bil-wadi" with the yā' retained in both states. ﴿And Pharaoh of the stakes﴾ is explained in Surah Sad [38:12]. ﴿Who transgressed in the lands﴾ means: Ad, Thamud and Pharaoh, who committed sins and acted tyrannically toward the prophets of God. ﴿And multiplied corruption therein﴾: killing and sins. ﴿So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment﴾. [(p-118)] Ibn Qutaybah said: He said "a scourge of punishment" because punishment may be by means of a whip. Al-Zajjaj said: [meaning, He made the whip with which He struck them the punishment]. ﴿Indeed your Lord is ever watchful﴾: He watches over whoever disbelieves in Him, to punish him. The "marsad" is the path, and we have explained it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is an ambush﴾ [an-Naba' 78:21].

﴿فَأَمَّا الْإِنْسَانُ﴾ [As for man]: there are four opinions about who is meant.

The first: 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: Umayyah ibn Khalaf. This was said by Muqatil.

(p-119) The fourth: that it refers to the disbeliever who does not believe in the Resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿وَابْتَلَاهُ﴾ means "tested him" (akhtabarahu), with wealth and ease. ﴿فَأَكْرَمَهُ﴾ means "honoured him" with wealth, and ﴿وَنَعَّمَهُ﴾ means "bestowed favour upon him" through the abundance of bounty he gave him. ﴿فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَكْرَمَنِ﴾ ("then says, 'My Lord has honoured me'"): the people of the Hijaz and Abu 'Amr read the ya' of ﴿رَبِّي﴾ and of ﴿أَكْرَمَنِيَ﴾ and ﴿أَهَانَنِيَ﴾ with a fatha (i.e. they pronounce them as rabbiya, akramaniya, ahananiya). The meaning is: He favoured me (faddalani) with what He gave me, and he thinks that what he was given of the world is because of his honour before Him. ﴿وَأَمَّا إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ﴾ ("But when He tests him") with poverty, ﴿فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ﴾ ("and restricts his provision"). Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿فَقَدَّرَ﴾ with a doubled dal (shadda). The meaning is: He narrowed his provision for him, by making it only the bare minimum (al-bulghah). ﴿فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَهَانَنِ﴾ ("then says, 'My Lord has humiliated me'"), meaning: this humiliation comes from Him to me, when He has abased me with poverty.

Know that whoever does not believe in the Resurrection, honour for him is an increase in worldly goods, and humiliation is a decrease in them.

(p-120) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿كَلَّا﴾ ("No!"), meaning: the matter is not as he supposes. Muqatil said: "I did not give this wealth to the one I made rich because of his honour before Me, nor did I make poor the one I made poor because of his humiliation before Me." Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that it was not fitting for him to be like this; rather, it was fitting for him to praise Allah for both states, poverty and wealth.

Then He informed about the disbelievers, saying: ﴿بَلْ لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ﴾ ("Rather, you do not honour the orphan"). The people of Basra read ﴿يُكْرِمُونَ﴾, ﴿يَحُضُّونَ﴾, ﴿يَأْكُلُونَ﴾ and ﴿يُحِبُّونَ﴾ with the ya' in all of them, while the rest read them with the ta' (tu-). The meaning of the verse: "I humiliated whom I humiliated because they did not honour the orphan." The verse may bear two meanings.

The first: that they did not show kindness to him.

The second: that they did not give him his right of inheritance. Likewise was the custom of the Jahiliyyah: they did not give inheritance to women or to children. The first meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَى طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ﴾ ("nor do you urge one another to feed the poor"). Abu Ja'far and the people of Kufa read ﴿تَحَاضُّونَ﴾ with an alif and a fatha on the ta'. Al-Shirazi narrated from al-Kisa'i the same, except that he put a damma on the ta'. The meaning: they do not command the feeding of the poor, because they do not hope for the reward of the Hereafter. The second meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿وَتَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَمًّا﴾ ("and you devour the inheritance with greedy devouring"). Ibn Qutaybah said: al-turath is the inheritance, and its ta' is changed from a waw, (p-121) as they say tujah, whose origin is wujah, and they say tukhamah, whose origin is wukhamah.

As for ﴿لَمًّا﴾, it means "intensely." It comes from your saying: lamamtu bi-l-shay' when you gather it together. Al-Zajjaj said: it means the inheritance of orphans.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ﴾ ("and you love wealth"), meaning: you love to gather it, ﴿حُبًّا جَمًّا﴾ ("with abundant love"), meaning: much. So you do not spend it in good. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ ("No!"), meaning: the matter should not be like this. Then He informed about their regret for what had passed from them, when it no longer benefits them, saying: ﴿إِذَا دُكَّتِ الْأَرْضُ دَكًّا دَكًّا﴾ ("When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded"), meaning: time after time, so that everything upon it is crushed. ﴿وَجَاءَ رَبُّكَ﴾ ("and your Lord comes"). We have mentioned this meaning in His saying: ﴿هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَّا أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("Do they await only that Allah should come to them…") [al-Baqarah: 210].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿وَالْمَلَكُ صَفًّا صَفًّا﴾ ("and the angels in ranks, rank upon rank"), meaning: the angels of each heaven come in separate rows, row after row. Al-Dahhak said: they will be seven rows. ﴿وَجِيءَ يَوْمَئِذٍ بِجَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("And on that Day Hell is brought"). Muslim narrated in his Afrad from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will be brought on that Day, having seventy thousand reins, and with each rein seventy thousand angels dragging it." (p-122) Muqatil said: it will be brought and placed to the left of the Throne.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ ("On that Day"), meaning: the Day when Hell is brought: ﴿يَتَذَكَّرُ الْإِنْسَانُ﴾ ("man will remember"), meaning: the disbeliever will take heed and repent. Muqatil said: he is Umayyah ibn Khalaf. ﴿وَأَنَّى لَهُ الذِّكْرَى﴾ ("and how will remembrance benefit him"), meaning: how can he have repentance, when it does not benefit in the Resurrection? ﴿يَقُولُ يَا لَيْتَنِي قَدَّمْتُ﴾ ("He will say, 'Would that I had sent ahead'") righteous deeds in the world ﴿لِحَيَاتِي﴾ ("for my life"), meaning: in the Hereafter, in which there is no death. ﴿فَيَوْمَئِذٍ لَا يُعَذِّبُ عَذَابَهُ أَحَدٌ﴾ ("On that Day none will punish as He punishes"). Al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and al-Mufaddal read ﴿لَا يُعَذَّبُ﴾ with a fatha on the dhal, while the rest read it with a kasra. Whoever reads with a fatha intends: none will punish the punishment of the disbeliever. Whoever reads with a kasra intends: none will punish the punishment of Allah, i.e., like His punishment. This reading is specific to the world, while the first reading is specific to the Hereafter.

(p-123) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿يَا أَيَّتُهَا النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ﴾ ("O soul at rest"). They differed about who it was revealed concerning, in five opinions.

The first: concerning Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib when he was martyred on the day of Uhud. This was said by Abu Hurayrah and Buraydah al-Aslami.

The second: concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan when he endowed the well of Rumah. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: concerning Khubayb ibn 'Adi when the people of Makkah crucified him. This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. This was related by al-Mawardi.

The fifth: concerning all the believers. This was said by Ikrimah.

As for the meaning of "al-Muti'innah" (the one at rest), there are three opinions.

The first: the believing soul. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Muti'innah means at rest with faith.

The second: the one content with the decree of Allah. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: the one certain of what Allah has promised. This was said by Qatadah.

They differed on the time at which it is said to her, in two opinions.

The first: at her departure from the world. This was said by most of them.

The second: at the Resurrection, it will be said to her: "Return to your companion, and to your body." Then Allah will command the spirits to return to the bodies. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said also by 'Ata', Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

(p-124) As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿ارْجِعِي إِلَى رَبِّكِ رَاضِيَةً﴾ ("Return to your Lord, well-pleased"), there are four opinions.

The first: "Return to your companion whose body you were in." This meaning is in the narration of al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

The second: ﴿ارْجِعِي إِلَى رَبِّكِ﴾ after death, in the world. This was said by Abu Salih.

The third: "Return to the reward of your Lord." This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: "O soul at rest [in the world], return to Allah, the Exalted, by leaving it." This was related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَادْخُلِي فِي عِبَادِي﴾ ("then enter among My servants"), meaning: among the whole body of My chosen servants. Abu Salih said: it is said to her at death, "Return to your Lord," and when the Day of Resurrection comes, it is said to her: ﴿فَادْخُلِي فِي عِبَادِي﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Enter with My servants." Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu al-Aliyah and Abu 'Imran read ﴿فِي عَبْدِي﴾ ("among My servant") in the singular. Al-Zajjaj said: according to this reading, and Allah knows best, the meaning is: "Return to your Lord," that is, to your companion from whom you departed, "then enter into him."

(p-125)

﴿فَأَمَّا الْإِنْسَانُ﴾ [As for man]: there are four opinions about who is meant.

The first: 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: Umayyah ibn Khalaf. This was said by Muqatil.

The meaning is: He favoured me (faddalani) with what He gave me, and he thinks that what he was given of the world is because of his honour before Him. ﴿وَأَمَّا إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ﴾ ("But when He tests him") with poverty, ﴿فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ﴾ ("and restricts his provision"). Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿فَقَدَّرَ﴾ with a doubled dal (shadda). The meaning is: He narrowed his provision for him, by making it only the bare minimum (al-bulghah). ﴿فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَهَانَنِ﴾ ("then says, 'My Lord has humiliated me'"), meaning: this humiliation comes from Him to me, when He has abased me with poverty.

Know that whoever does not believe in the Resurrection, honour for him is an increase in worldly goods, and humiliation is a decrease in them.

(p-120) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿كَلَّا﴾ ("No!"), meaning: the matter is not as he supposes. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that it was not fitting for him to be like this; rather, it was fitting for him to praise Allah for both states, poverty and wealth.

The meaning of the verse: "I humiliated whom I humiliated because they did not honour the orphan." The verse may bear two meanings.

The first: that they did not show kindness to him.

The second: that they did not give him his right of inheritance. Likewise was the custom of the Jahiliyyah: they did not give inheritance to women or to children. The first meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَى طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ﴾ ("nor do you urge one another to feed the poor"). The meaning is: He favoured me (faddalani) with what He gave me, and he thinks that what he was given of the world is because of his honour before Him. ﴿وَأَمَّا إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ﴾ ("But when He tests him") with poverty, ﴿فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ﴾ ("and restricts his provision"). The first: that they did not show kindness to him.

(p-124) As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿ارْجِعِي إِلَى رَبِّكِ رَاضِيَةً﴾ ("Return to your Lord, well-pleased"), there are four opinions.

The first: "Return to your companion whose body you were in." This meaning is in the narration of al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

The second: ﴿ارْجِعِي إِلَى رَبِّكِ﴾ after death, in the world. This was said by Abu Salih.

The third: "Return to the reward of your Lord." This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: "O soul at rest [in the world], return to Allah, the Exalted, by leaving it." This was related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَادْخُلِي فِي عِبَادِي﴾ ("then enter among My servants"), meaning: among the whole body of My chosen servants. Abu Salih said: it is said to her at death, "Return to your Lord," and when the Day of Resurrection comes, it is said to her: ﴿فَادْخُلِي فِي عِبَادِي﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Enter with My servants." Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu al-Aliyah and Abu 'Imran read ﴿فِي عَبْدِي﴾ ("among My servant") in the singular. Al-Zajjaj said: according to this reading, and Allah knows best, the meaning is: "Return to your Lord," that is, to your companion from whom you departed, "then enter into him."

(p-125)

﴿فَأَمَّا الْإِنْسَانُ﴾ [As for man]: there are four opinions about who is meant.

The first: 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: Umayyah ibn Khalaf. This was said by Muqatil.

(p-119) The fourth: that it refers to the disbeliever who does not believe in the Resurrection. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿وَابْتَلَاهُ﴾ means "tested him" (akhtabarahu), with wealth and ease. ﴿فَأَكْرَمَهُ﴾ means "honoured him" with wealth, and ﴿وَنَعَّمَهُ﴾ means "bestowed favour upon him" through the abundance of bounty he gave him. ﴿فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَكْرَمَنِ﴾ ("then says, 'My Lord has honoured me'"): the people of the Hijaz and Abu 'Amr read the ya' of ﴿رَبِّي﴾ and of ﴿أَكْرَمَنِيَ﴾ and ﴿أَهَانَنِيَ﴾ with a fatha (i.e. they pronounce them as rabbiya, akramaniya, ahananiya). The meaning is: He favoured me (faddalani) with what He gave me, and he thinks that what he was given of the world is because of his honour before Him. ﴿وَأَمَّا إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ﴾ ("But when He tests him") with poverty, ﴿فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ﴾ ("and restricts his provision"). Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿فَقَدَّرَ﴾ with a doubled dal (shadda). The meaning is: He narrowed his provision for him, by making it only the bare minimum (al-bulghah). ﴿فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَهَانَنِ﴾ ("then says, 'My Lord has humiliated me'"), meaning: this humiliation comes from Him to me, when He has abased me with poverty.

Know that whoever does not believe in the Resurrection, honour for him is an increase in worldly goods, and humiliation is a decrease in them.

(p-120) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿كَلَّا﴾ ("No!"), meaning: the matter is not as he supposes. Muqatil said: "I did not give this wealth to the one I made rich because of his honour before Me, nor did I make poor the one I made poor because of his humiliation before Me." Al-Farra' said: the meaning is that it was not fitting for him to be like this; rather, it was fitting for him to praise Allah for both states, poverty and wealth.

Then He informed about the disbelievers, saying: ﴿بَلْ لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ﴾ ("Rather, you do not honour the orphan"). The people of Basra read ﴿يُكْرِمُونَ﴾, ﴿يَحُضُّونَ﴾, ﴿يَأْكُلُونَ﴾ and ﴿يُحِبُّونَ﴾ with the ya' in all of them, while the rest read them with the ta' (tu-). The meaning of the verse: "I humiliated whom I humiliated because they did not honour the orphan." The verse may bear two meanings.

The first: that they did not show kindness to him.

The second: that they did not give him his right of inheritance. Likewise was the custom of the Jahiliyyah: they did not give inheritance to women or to children. The first meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَى طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ﴾ ("nor do you urge one another to feed the poor"). Abu Ja'far and the people of Kufa read ﴿تَحَاضُّونَ﴾ with an alif and a fatha on the ta'. Al-Shirazi narrated from al-Kisa'i the same, except that he put a damma on the ta'. The meaning: they do not command the feeding of the poor, because they do not hope for the reward of the Hereafter. The second meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿وَتَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَمًّا﴾ ("and you devour the inheritance with greedy devouring"). Ibn Qutaybah said: al-turath is the inheritance, and its ta' is changed from a waw, (p-121) as they say tujah, whose origin is wujah, and they say tukhamah, whose origin is wukhamah.

As for ﴿لَمًّا﴾, it means "intensely." It comes from your saying: lamamtu bi-l-shay' when you gather it together. Al-Zajjaj said: it means the inheritance of orphans.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ﴾ ("and you love wealth"), meaning: you love to gather it, ﴿حُبًّا جَمًّا﴾ ("with abundant love"), meaning: much. So you do not spend it in good. ﴿كَلَّا﴾ ("No!"), meaning: the matter should not be like this. Then He informed about their regret for what had passed from them, when it no longer benefits them, saying: ﴿إِذَا دُكَّتِ الْأَرْضُ دَكًّا دَكًّا﴾ ("When the earth is pounded to powder, pounded"), meaning: time after time, so that everything upon it is crushed. ﴿وَجَاءَ رَبُّكَ﴾ ("and your Lord comes"). We have mentioned this meaning in His saying: ﴿هَلْ يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَّا أَنْ يَأْتِيَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("Do they await only that Allah should come to them…") [al-Baqarah: 210].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿وَالْمَلَكُ صَفًّا صَفًّا﴾ ("and the angels in ranks, rank upon rank"), meaning: the angels of each heaven come in separate rows, row after row. Al-Dahhak said: they will be seven rows. ﴿وَجِيءَ يَوْمَئِذٍ بِجَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("And on that Day Hell is brought"). Muslim narrated in his Afrad from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will be brought on that Day, having seventy thousand reins, and with each rein seventy thousand angels dragging it." (p-122) Muqatil said: it will be brought and placed to the left of the Throne.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ﴾ ("On that Day"), meaning: the Day when Hell is brought: ﴿يَتَذَكَّرُ الْإِنْسَانُ﴾ ("man will remember"), meaning: the disbeliever will take heed and repent. Muqatil said: he is Umayyah ibn Khalaf. ﴿وَأَنَّى لَهُ الذِّكْرَى﴾ ("and how will remembrance benefit him"), meaning: how can he have repentance, when it does not benefit in the Resurrection? ﴿يَقُولُ يَا لَيْتَنِي قَدَّمْتُ﴾ ("He will say, 'Would that I had sent ahead'") righteous deeds in the world ﴿لِحَيَاتِي﴾ ("for my life"), meaning: in the Hereafter, in which there is no death. ﴿فَيَوْمَئِذٍ لَا يُعَذِّبُ عَذَابَهُ أَحَدٌ﴾ ("On that Day none will punish as He punishes"). Al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and al-Mufaddal read ﴿لَا يُعَذَّبُ﴾ with a fatha on the dhal, while the rest read it with a kasra. Whoever reads with a fatha intends: none will punish the punishment of the disbeliever. Whoever reads with a kasra intends: none will punish the punishment of Allah, i.e., like His punishment. This reading is specific to the world, while the first reading is specific to the Hereafter.

(p-123) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿يَا أَيَّتُهَا النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ﴾ ("O soul at rest"). They differed about who it was revealed concerning, in five opinions.

The first: concerning Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib when he was martyred on the day of Uhud. This was said by Abu Hurayrah and Buraydah al-Aslami.

The second: concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan when he endowed the well of Rumah. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: concerning Khubayb ibn 'Adi when the people of Makkah crucified him. This was said by Muqatil.

The fourth: concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. This was related by al-Mawardi.

The fifth: concerning all the believers. This was said by Ikrimah.

As for the meaning of "al-Muti'innah" (the one at rest), there are three opinions.

The first: the believing soul. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Muti'innah means at rest with faith.

The second: the one content with the decree of Allah. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: the one certain of what Allah has promised. This was said by Qatadah.

They differed on the time at which it is said to her, in two opinions.

The first: at her departure from the world. This was said by most of them.

The second: at the Resurrection, it will be said to her: "Return to your companion, and to your body." Then Allah will command the spirits to return to the bodies. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said also by 'Ata', Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

(p-124) As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿ارْجِعِي إِلَى رَبِّكِ رَاضِيَةً﴾ ("Return to your Lord, well-pleased"), there are four opinions.

The first: "Return to your companion whose body you were in." This meaning is in the narration of al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and it was said by Ikrimah and al-Dahhak.

The second: ﴿ارْجِعِي إِلَى رَبِّكِ﴾ after death, in the world. This was said by Abu Salih.

The third: "Return to the reward of your Lord." This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: "O soul at rest [in the world], return to Allah, the Exalted, by leaving it." This was related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿فَادْخُلِي فِي عِبَادِي﴾ ("then enter among My servants"), meaning: among the whole body of My chosen servants. Abu Salih said: it is said to her at death, "Return to your Lord," and when the Day of Resurrection comes, it is said to her: ﴿فَادْخُلِي فِي عِبَادِي﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Enter with My servants." Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu al-Aliyah and Abu 'Imran read ﴿فِي عَبْدِي﴾ ("among My servant") in the singular. Al-Zajjaj said: according to this reading, and Allah knows best, the meaning is: "Return to your Lord," that is, to your companion from whom you departed, "then enter into him."

(p-125)
